claim: Slo1 is a Ca2+- and voltage-activated K+ channel that underlies skeletal and smooth muscle contraction, audition, hormone secretion and neurotransmitter release.
source: Slo1 is a Ca2+- and voltage-activated K+ channel that underlies skeletal and smooth muscle contraction, audition, hormone secretion and neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these physiological roles.

claim: In mammals, Slo1 is regulated by auxiliary proteins that confer tissue-specific gating and pharmacological properties.
source: In mammals, Slo1 is regulated by auxiliary proteins that confer tissue-specific gating and pharmacological properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: This study presents cryo-EM structures of Slo1 in complex with the auxiliary protein, β4.
source: This study presents cryo-EM structures of Slo1 in complex with the auxiliary protein, β4.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four β4, each containing two transmembrane helices, encircle Slo1, contacting it through helical interactions inside the membrane.
source: Four β4, each containing two transmembrane helices, encircle Slo1, contacting it through helical interactions inside the membrane.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data and models presented in the manuscript.

claim: On the extracellular side, β4 forms a tetrameric crown over the pore.
source: On the extracellular side, β4 forms a tetrameric crown over the pore.
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Structures with high and low Ca2+ concentrations show that identical gating conformations occur in the absence and presence of β4.
source: Structures with high and low Ca2+ concentrations show that identical gating conformations occur in the absence and presence of β4, implying that β4 serves to modulate the relative stabilities of 'pre-existing' conformations rather than creating new ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparisons presented in the manuscript.

claim: β4 serves to modulate the relative stabilities of 'pre-existing' conformations rather than creating new ones.
source: Structures with high and low Ca2+ concentrations show that identical gating conformations occur in the absence and presence of β4, implying that β4 serves to modulate the relative stabilities of 'pre-existing' conformations rather than creating new ones.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data showing identical conformations with and without β4.

claim: The effects of β4 on scorpion toxin inhibition kinetics are explained by the crown, which constrains access but does not prevent binding.
source: The effects of β4 on scorpion toxin inhibition kinetics are explained by the crown, which constrains access but does not prevent binding.
evidence: This mechanistic explanation is based on structural modeling and inference from the crown structure.

claim: The Slo1 channel distinguishes itself from other K+ channels by its unusually large single-channel conductance (~10–20 times greater than most other K+ channels).
source: The Slo1 channel, also known as BK or MaxiK, distinguishes itself from other K+ channels by its unusually large single-channel conductance (~10–20 times greater than most other K+ channels) and dual regulation by intracellular Ca2+ and membrane voltage (Marty, 1981; Pallotta et al., 1981; Barrett et al., 1982; Latorre et al., 1982; Latorre and Miller, 1983; Elkins et al., 1986; Atkinson et al., 1991; Adelman et al., 1992; Butler et al., 1993; Pallanck and Ganetzky, 1994; Magleby, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Slo1 is dually regulated by intracellular Ca2+ and membrane voltage.
source: The Slo1 channel, also known as BK or MaxiK, distinguishes itself from other K+ channels by its unusually large single-channel conductance (~10–20 times greater than most other K+ channels) and dual regulation by intracellular Ca2+ and membrane voltage (Marty, 1981; Pallotta et al., 1981; Barrett et al., 1982; Latorre et al., 1982; Latorre and Miller, 1983; Elkins et al., 1986; Atkinson et al., 1991; Adelman et al., 1992; Butler et al., 1993; Pallanck and Ganetzky, 1994; Magleby, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Slo1 serves as a hub in numerous physiological processes that couple membrane excitability to Ca2+ signaling events such as muscle contraction, audition, hormone secretion, and neurotransmitter release.
source: Because both Ca2+ and membrane voltage gate Slo1, it serves as a hub in numerous physiological processes that couple membrane excitability to Ca2+ signaling events such as muscle contraction, audition, hormone secretion, and neurotransmitter release (Contreras et al., 2013; Latorre et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deficiencies in the Slo1 channel have been linked to a spectrum of diseases including hypertension, urinary incontinence secondary to overactive bladder (OAB), epilepsy, mental retardation, and autism.
source: Deficiencies in the Slo1 channel have been linked to a spectrum of diseases including hypertension, urinary incontinence secondary to overactive bladder (OAB), epilepsy, mental retardation, and autism (Contreras et al., 2013; Latorre et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Slo1 functions as a tetramer of the pore-forming α subunit, which is encoded by a single gene, Slowpoke (KCNMA1).
source: Slo1 functions as a tetramer of the pore-forming α subunit, which is encoded by a single gene, Slowpoke (KCNMA1).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Previously determined atomic structures of aplysia Slo1 provided an explanation for the apparent paradox of an unusually high conductance and exquisite K+ selectivity.
source: Previously, we determined the atomic structures of aplysia Slo1(acSlo1) in the absence and presence of Ca2+ (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017). These structures provided an explanation for the apparent paradox of an unusually high conductance and exquisite K+ selectivity, showed how the Ca2+ sensing mechanism can work, and showed how the Ca2+ and voltage sensors are in contact with each other, allowing for the possibility that the two sensing mechanisms could be directly coupled (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Previously determined atomic structures of aplysia Slo1 showed how the Ca2+ sensing mechanism can work.
source: Previously, we determined the atomic structures of aplysia Slo1(acSlo1) in the absence and presence of Ca2+ (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017). These structures provided an explanation for the apparent paradox of an unusually high conductance and exquisite K+ selectivity, showed how the Ca2+ sensing mechanism can work, and showed how the Ca2+ and voltage sensors are in contact with each other, allowing for the possibility that the two sensing mechanisms could be directly coupled (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Previously determined atomic structures of aplysia Slo1 showed how the Ca2+ and voltage sensors are in contact with each other, allowing for the possibility that the two sensing mechanisms could be directly coupled.
source: Previously, we determined the atomic structures of aplysia Slo1(acSlo1) in the absence and presence of Ca2+ (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017). These structures provided an explanation for the apparent paradox of an unusually high conductance and exquisite K+ selectivity, showed how the Ca2+ sensing mechanism can work, and showed how the Ca2+ and voltage sensors are in contact with each other, allowing for the possibility that the two sensing mechanisms could be directly coupled (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: In mammals, Slo1 channels usually consist of α plus auxiliary subunits.
source: In mammals, Slo1 channels usually consist of α plus auxiliary subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The α subunits of mammalian Slo1 are similar to those of invertebrate Slo1 channels.
source: The α subunits are similar to those of invertebrate Slo1 channels, but the auxiliary subunits represent a novel feature.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and structural comparisons.

claim: Auxiliary subunits give rise to functional diversity and to tissue-specificity amongst the otherwise ubiquitously expressed Slo1 channel α subunit.
source: Auxiliary subunits give rise to functional diversity and to tissue-specificity amongst the otherwise ubiquitously expressed Slo1 channel α subunit.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: There are two distinct families of auxiliary subunits discovered so far, termed β (2-transmembrane, 2-TM) and γ (single-TM).
source: There are two distinct families of auxiliary subunits discovered so far, termed β (2-transmembrane, 2-TM) and γ (single-TM) (Garcia-Calvo et al., 1994; Knaus et al., 1994b; Knaus et al., 1994c; Behrens et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2000; Meera et al., 2000; Uebele et al., 2000; Weiger et al., 2000; Xia et al., 2000; Braun, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2012; Zhang and Yan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Auxiliary subunits diversify the function of Slo1 to the greatest extent compared to other modifications such as alternative splicing, phosphorylation etc.
source: These auxiliary subunits diversify the function of Slo1 to the greatest extent compared to other modifications such as alternative splicing, phosphorylation etc.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Auxiliary subunits dramatically modify nearly all aspects of Slo1's biophysical properties (including the activation and deactivation kinetics and Ca2+ sensitivity) as well as pharmacological characteristics (such as the channel's sensitivity to natural toxins).
source: They dramatically modify nearly all aspects of Slo1's biophysical properties (including the activation and deactivation kinetics and Ca2+ sensitivity) as well as pharmacological characteristics (such as the channel's sensitivity to natural toxins) (McManus et al., 1995; Dworetzky et al., 1996; Chang et al., 1997; Orio et al., 2002; Lippiat et al., 2003; Ha et al., 2004; Brenner et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2006; Savalli et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2008; Braun, 2010; Wu and Marx, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2010; Yan and Aldrich, 2012; Torres et al., 2014; Zhang and Yan, 2014; Latorre et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: There are four members identified for each family (β1-β4 and γ1-γ4).
source: There are four members identified for each family (β1-β4 and γ1-γ4) and members within the same family modify channel function to very different extents.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Members within the same family modify channel function to very different extents.
source: There are four members identified for each family (β1-β4 and γ1-γ4) and members within the same family modify channel function to very different extents.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Auxiliary subunits generally do not exist in lower animals.
source: These auxiliary subunits generally do not exist in lower animals.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Regulation of Slo1 by auxiliary subunits appears to be a key mechanism of functional tuning to fulfill different physiological roles in various tissues and cell types of higher animals.
source: Therefore, regulation of Slo1 by auxiliary subunits appears to be a key mechanism of functional tuning to fulfill different physiological roles in various tissues and cell types of higher animals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional diversity conferred by auxiliary subunits.

claim: No structure of a β or γ subunit alone or in complex with the α subunit has been determined prior to this study.
source: So far, no structure of a β or γ subunit alone or in complex with the α subunit has been determined to help us understand how these proteins work.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: This study presents the structures of a mammalian (human) Slo1 channel consisting of the α subunit alone and in complex with the brain-enriched β4 subunit.
source: In this study we present the structures of a mammalian (human) Slo1 channel consisting of the α subunit alone and in complex with the brain-enriched β4 subunit.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by the structural data.

claim: In each case (presence and absence of β4 subunit) structures of Ca2+-activated (open) and Ca2+-depleted (closed) conformations were determined.
source: In each case (presence and absence of β4 subunit) we have determined the structures of Ca2+-activated (open) and Ca2+-depleted (closed) conformations.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by the structural data.

claim: The study interrogates the influence of structure-guided mutations of β4 using an electrophysiological assay.
source: We also interrogate the influence of structure-guided mutations of β4 using an electrophysiological assay.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by the functional data.

claim: The gene encoding the Slo1 α subunit was modified by removing the C-terminal 57 amino acids (unstructured in the crystal structure of the human Slo1 cytoplasmic domain).
source: To obtain biochemically stable protein samples suitable for structural studies we modified the gene encoding the Slo1 α subunit by removing the C-terminal 57 amino acids (unstructured in the crystal structure of the human Slo1 cytoplasmic domain) (Yuan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citation to prior structural work.

claim: This modification neither affected the function of the Slo1 channel α subunit alone nor the functional influence β subunits have on Slo1.
source: This modification neither affected the function of the Slo1 channel α subunit alone nor the functional influence β subunits have on Slo1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-expression with either the β1 or β4 subunit slowed the activation and deactivation kinetics of the truncated Slo1 channel.
source: Co-expression with either the β1 or β4 subunit slowed the activation and deactivation kinetics of the truncated Slo1 channel and modified its apparent Ca2+sensitivity, as reported for the full length Slo1 channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (McManus et al., 1995; Dworetzky et al., 1996; Lippiat et al., 2003; Ha et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Co-expression with either the β1 or β4 subunit modified the apparent Ca2+ sensitivity of the truncated Slo1 channel.
source: Co-expression with either the β1 or β4 subunit slowed the activation and deactivation kinetics of the truncated Slo1 channel and modified its apparent Ca2+sensitivity, as reported for the full length Slo1 channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (McManus et al., 1995; Dworetzky et al., 1996; Lippiat et al., 2003; Ha et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: Structures of human Slo1 in four distinct states were determined: Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound α subunit alone as well as Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound α-β4 complex at resolutions of 4.0 Å, 3.8 Å, 3.5 Å and 3.2 Å, respectively.
source: Structures of human Slo1 in four distinct states were determined: Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound α subunit alone as well as Ca2+-free and Ca2+-bound α-β4 complex at resolutions of 4.0 Å, 3.8 Å, 3.5 Å and 3.2 Å, respectively (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 2–4 and Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated and supported by the structural data and figures.

claim: The human Slo1 α subunit tetramer is organized similarly to acSlo1.
source: The human Slo1 α subunit tetramer is organized similarly to acSlo1 (Figure 1B) (Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison and citation to prior work.

claim: Four of the β4 subunits bind to the human Slo1 tetramer, extending the channel extracellularly by about 40 Å when viewed from the side.
source: Four of the β4 subunits bind to the human Slo1 tetramer, extending the channel extracellularly by about 40 Å when viewed from the side (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The complex has dimensions of approximately 150×150×150 Å.
source: The complex has dimensions of approximately 150×150×150 Å.
evidence: This is a measurement derived from the structural data.

claim: β4 subunits are located between voltage sensor domains (VSDs) and each β4 subunit contacts two neighboring VSDs simultaneously.
source: Consistent with disulfide crosslinking data in the literature, β4 subunits are located between voltage sensor domains (VSDs) and each β4 subunit contacts two neighboring VSDs simultaneously (Figure 1B) (Liu et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and is consistent with prior biochemical studies.

claim: Four EC domains form a 'crown' on top of the Slo1 channel.
source: Four EC domains form a 'crown' on top of the Slo1 channel (Figure 1B).
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The protein sample contained high concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+ (10 mM each).
source: The protein sample contained high concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+ (10 mM each).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about sample preparation.

claim: The channel adopts an open conformation under high Ca2+ and Mg2+ conditions.
source: As expected, the channel adopts an open conformation and both Ca2+ binding sites (the Ca-RCK1 site and the Ca-bowl site) in the gating ring and the Mg2+ binding site at the interface between RCK1 and the VSD are occupied, as observed in acSlo1 under the same buffer conditions (Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and comparison to prior work.

claim: Both Ca2+ binding sites (the Ca-RCK1 site and the Ca-bowl site) in the gating ring are occupied under high Ca2+ conditions.
source: As expected, the channel adopts an open conformation and both Ca2+ binding sites (the Ca-RCK1 site and the Ca-bowl site) in the gating ring and the Mg2+ binding site at the interface between RCK1 and the VSD are occupied, as observed in acSlo1 under the same buffer conditions (Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and comparison to prior work.

claim: The Mg2+ binding site at the interface between RCK1 and the VSD is occupied under high Mg2+ conditions.
source: As expected, the channel adopts an open conformation and both Ca2+ binding sites (the Ca-RCK1 site and the Ca-bowl site) in the gating ring and the Mg2+ binding site at the interface between RCK1 and the VSD are occupied, as observed in acSlo1 under the same buffer conditions (Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data and comparison to prior work.

claim: The β4 subunit contains two long transmembrane helices, TM1 and TM2.
source: As predicted from the primary sequence, the β4 subunit contains two long transmembrane helices, TM1 and TM2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with sequence predictions.

claim: Density for the N-terminal six amino acids as well as the C-terminal five amino acids (residues 206–210) were not visible in the open Slo1-β4 complex, indicating their structural flexibility.
source: Density for the N-terminal six amino acids as well as the C-terminal five amino acids (residues 206–210) were not visible in the open Slo1-β4 complex, indicating their structural flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Amino acids 7–11 form a short loop (termed 'N-loop') preceding TM1.
source: Amino acids 7–11 form a short loop (termed 'N-loop') preceding TM1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TM1 kinks near the extracellular membrane interface and extends further into the extracellular space about four additional helical turns.
source: TM1 kinks near the extracellular membrane interface and extends further into the extracellular space about four additional helical turns while TM2 extends beyond the intracellular membrane interface into the cytoplasm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TM2 extends beyond the intracellular membrane interface into the cytoplasm.
source: TM1 kinks near the extracellular membrane interface and extends further into the extracellular space about four additional helical turns while TM2 extends beyond the intracellular membrane interface into the cytoplasm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TM1 and TM2 within the β4 monomer form an extensive interface with mostly hydrophobic interactions.
source: TM1 and TM2 within the β4 monomer form an extensive interface with mostly hydrophobic interactions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The extended C-terminal part of TM2 also interacts with the N-loop through a few hydrogen bonds.
source: The extended C-terminal part of TM2 also interacts with the N-loop through a few hydrogen bonds (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The EC domain of β4 subunit contains mostly β strands (βA-βE, βH-βI), two short α helices (αF-αG) and loops in between.
source: The well-ordered EC domain, which connects TM1 and TM2, contains mostly β strands (βA-βE, βH-βI), two short α helices (αF-αG) and loops in between (Figure 2A and C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 2A, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The structure is held together by four disulfide bonds.
source: The structure is held together by four disulfide bonds (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The β4 EC domain contains two predicted N-glycosylation sites, with one of them conserved among all the β subunits.
source: The β4 EC domain also contains two predicted N-glycosylation sites, with one of them conserved among all the β subunits (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and structural data.

claim: Glycosylation at these two predicted sites were confirmed with tandem ms/ms.
source: Glycosylation at these two predicted sites were confirmed with tandem ms/ms and extra density near both sites was observed in the final map, most likely representing the sugars.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and cryo-EM density.

claim: Extra density near both glycosylation sites was observed in the final map, most likely representing the sugars.
source: Glycosylation at these two predicted sites were confirmed with tandem ms/ms and extra density near both sites was observed in the final map, most likely representing the sugars.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cryo-EM density and mass spectrometry data.

claim: Glycosylation was shown to regulate the sensitivity of Slo1-β4 to iberiotoxin and also modify other biophysical properties of Slo1-β1.
source: Glycosylation was shown to regulate the sensitivity of Slo1-β4 to iberiotoxin and also modify other biophysical properties of Slo1-β1 (Jin et al., 2002; Hagen and Sanders, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the open Slo1-β4 model, these two glycosylation sites are located at the outer periphery of the EC domain, far from the β4/β4 or α/β4 interfaces.
source: In the open Slo1-β4 model, these two glycosylation sites are located at the outer periphery of the EC domain, far from the β4/β4 or α/β4 interfaces (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The structure does not obviously explain the functional effects of glycosylation modifications.
source: Therefore, the structure does not obviously explain the functional effects of these modifications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of the glycosylation sites.

claim: Proteins in this study were expressed using a glycosylation-deficient strain that produces smaller sugar groups.
source: We note that proteins in this study were expressed using a glycosylation-deficient strain that produces smaller sugar groups.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about protein expression.

claim: The secondary structural elements as well as the four disulfide bonds match a recently published NMR structure of the extracellular loop of human β4.
source: The secondary structural elements as well as the four disulfide bonds match a recently published NMR structure of the extracellular loop of human β4 (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to a prior NMR structure.

claim: The Slo1-β4 complex structure exhibits a completely different tertiary structure of the EC domain than that proposed on the basis of NMR experiments.
source: However, our Slo1-β4 complex structure exhibits a completely different tertiary structure of the EC domain than that proposed on the basis of NMR experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current structure and a prior NMR-based model.

claim: N123 on β4 and E264 on the turret of the α subunit are more than 27 Å apart in the open Slo1-β4 complex structure.
source: However, these two residues are more than 27 Å apart in our open Slo1-β4 complex structure and remained essentially static in the closed Slo1-β4 complex structure, making any direct interactions very unlikely.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structural data.

claim: N123 on β4 and E264 on the turret of the α subunit remained essentially static in the closed Slo1-β4 complex structure.
source: However, these two residues are more than 27 Å apart in our open Slo1-β4 complex structure and remained essentially static in the closed Slo1-β4 complex structure, making any direct interactions very unlikely.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the open and closed structures.

claim: Direct interactions between N123 on β4 and E264 on the turret of the α subunit are very unlikely.
source: However, these two residues are more than 27 Å apart in our open Slo1-β4 complex structure and remained essentially static in the closed Slo1-β4 complex structure, making any direct interactions very unlikely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distance measurements from the structural data.

claim: No structural homologs of the EC domain have been reported.
source: No structural homologs of the EC domain have been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge based on database searches.

claim: The stoichiometry of α and β subunits was assumed generally to be 1:1.
source: The stoichiometry of α and β subunits was assumed generally to be 1:1.
evidence: This is a statement about prior assumptions in the field.

claim: Evidence of sub 1:1 stoichiometry emerged from analysis of co-expression in oocytes as well as in native tissues.
source: Evidence of sub 1:1 stoichiometry emerged from analysis of co-expression in oocytes (Wang et al., 2002) as well as in native tissues (Solaro et al., 1995; Ding et al., 1998; Kuntamallappanavar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It was proposed that a Slo1 channel can contain zero to four β subunits, with each β subunit incrementally influencing channel gating properties.
source: It was proposed that a Slo1 channel can contain zero to four β subunits, with each β subunit incrementally influencing channel gating properties (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In the Slo1-β4 complex structure, β4 binds to the α subunit with 1:1 subunit stoichiometry (i.e. four β4 subunits per tetramer of α subunits).
source: In the Slo1-β4 complex structure, β4 binds to the α subunit with 1:1 subunit stoichiometry (i.e. four β4 subunits per tetramer of α subunits) (Figures 1B and 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 1B and 2D-E.

claim: The four β4 subunits form extensive interfaces with neighboring EC domains, encompassing a buried area of ~907 Å2/monomer.
source: The four β4 subunits form extensive interfaces with neighboring EC domains, encompassing a buried area of ~907 Å2/monomer (Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This is a measurement derived from the structural data shown in Figures 2D-G.

claim: The structure would predict a more stable conformation upon tetramer formation because the EC domain, which interacts extensively with itself, makes only minimal contact with the α subunit.
source: However, the structure would predict a more stable conformation upon tetramer formation because the EC domain, which interacts extensively with itself, makes only minimal contact with the α subunit (Figures 1B and 2D–G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing extensive β4-β4 interactions.

claim: TM1 was predicted to be in the vicinity of S1 and S2 on the VSD.
source: TM1 was predicted to be in the vicinity of S1 and S2 on the VSD (Liu et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2013) and direct interactions between TM1 of β2 and S1 of the VSD were found using the TOXCAT assay (Morera et al., 2012).

claim: Direct interactions between TM1 of β2 and S1 of the VSD were found using the TOXCAT assay.
source: TM1 was predicted to be in the vicinity of S1 and S2 on the VSD (Liu et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2013) and direct interactions between TM1 of β2 and S1 of the VSD were found using the TOXCAT assay (Morera et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: In the Slo1-β4 structure, β4 associates with the α subunit almost exclusively through the two TM helices.
source: In our Slo1-β4 structure, β4 associates with the α subunit almost exclusively through the two TM helices (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TM1 segment near the outer leaflet of the membrane contacts the transmembrane domain (TMD) from one α subunit ('α1') through hydrophobic interactions with sidechains from S1 and the pore helix (PH), while at the same time interacting with sidechains from S6 and the turret of a contiguous α subunit ('α2').
source: The TM1 segment near the outer leaflet of the membrane contacts the transmembrane domain (TMD) from one α subunit ('α1') through hydrophobic interactions with sidechains from S1 and the pore helix (PH), while at the same time interacting with sidechains from S6 and the turret of a contiguous α subunit ('α2') (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Lipid molecules also contribute to the interfaces between β4 and α subunits.
source: Notably, lipid molecules also contribute to these interfaces (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: The TM1 segment near the inner leaflet acyl chain region mostly contacts S3 of α2 and several ordered lipid molecules through hydrophobic interactions.
source: The TM1 segment near the inner leaflet acyl chain region mostly contacts S3 of α2 and several ordered lipid molecules through hydrophobic interactions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The bottom of TM1, near the intracellular membrane interface, makes contacts with multiple regions of the α subunit including the S2-S3 linker and S0 from α2, the S6-RCK1 linker from α1 and phospholipid headgroups through hydrogen bonds.
source: The bottom of TM1, near the intracellular membrane interface, makes contacts with multiple regions of the α subunit including the S2-S3 linker and S0 from α2, the S6-RCK1 linker from α1 and phospholipid headgroups through hydrogen bonds (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No direct association with the α subunit was detected for TM2 using the TOXCAT assay.
source: With the same TOXCAT assay, no direct association with the α subunit was detected for TM2, the EC domain, or the C-terminus of β and it was thus suggested that there are no strong interactions between TM2 and S0 despite the nearness predicted from the disulfide crosslinking experiments (Liu et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010; Morera et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The structure shows that the TM2 outer leaflet segment only interacts with α2 and this interface is purely mediated by lipid molecules forming a hydrophobic core with TM2 sidechains.
source: Our structure shows that the TM2 outer leaflet segment only interacts with α2. Furthermore, this interface is purely mediated by lipid molecules forming a hydrophobic core with TM2 sidechains (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: The TM2 inner leaflet segment forms an extensive protein:protein interface with S0 and S3 from α2.
source: The TM2 inner leaflet segment forms an extensive protein:protein interface with S0 and S3 from α2 (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 3A and 3C.

claim: The residues of β4 directly involved in the α/β association turn out to be fairly conserved among β1-β4.
source: The residues of β4 directly involved in the α/β association turn out to be fairly conserved among β1-β4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: It would seem likely that β1-β4 subunits all bind to Slo1 in a similar fashion.
source: Therefore, it would seem likely that β1-β4 subunits all bind to Slo1 in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation of binding residues.

claim: Slo1 residues involved in these specific interactions appear to be conserved between Slo1 and Slo3.
source: Furthermore, Slo1 residues involved in these specific interactions appear to be conserved between Slo1 and Slo3, which would explain why all members of the β subunit family also physically associate with Slo3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment and citation to prior literature.

claim: All members of the β subunit family also physically associate with Slo3.
source: Furthermore, Slo1 residues involved in these specific interactions appear to be conserved between Slo1 and Slo3, which would explain why all members of the β subunit family also physically associate with Slo3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) (Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Lipid molecules make significant contributions to the α/β interfaces at both the inner and outer membrane leaflets.
source: We emphasize the general observation that lipid molecules make significant contributions to the α/β interfaces at both the inner and outer membrane leaflets, suggesting they are an integral part of the Slo1 α-β4 channel complex (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lipid molecules are an integral part of the Slo1 α-β4 channel complex.
source: We emphasize the general observation that lipid molecules make significant contributions to the α/β interfaces at both the inner and outer membrane leaflets, suggesting they are an integral part of the Slo1 α-β4 channel complex (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the extensive lipid-mediated interactions observed in the structure.

claim: In the open α-β4 model, the N-loop preceding TM1 is located adjacent to the S6-RCK1 linker and the αC helix of the RCK1 N-lobe.
source: In the open α-β4 model, the N-loop preceding TM1 is located adjacent to the S6-RCK1 linker and the αC helix of the RCK1 N-lobe, making short and long-range interactions between these regions likely.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: Short and long-range interactions between the N-loop and the S6-RCK1 linker and the αC helix of the RCK1 N-lobe are likely.
source: In the open α-β4 model, the N-loop preceding TM1 is located adjacent to the S6-RCK1 linker and the αC helix of the RCK1 N-lobe, making short and long-range interactions between these regions likely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proximity observed in the structure.

claim: T11 of β4 is less than 5 Å away from D173 in the S2-S3 loop of the α subunit.
source: T11 of β4 is less than 5 Å away from D173 in the S2-S3 loop of the α subunit; the E12 sidechain of β4 is about 5.5 Å away from R329 in the S6-RCK1 linker and is also in the vicinity of W176 on S3 and H409 on the αC helix.
evidence: This is a distance measurement from the structural data.

claim: The E12 sidechain of β4 is about 5.5 Å away from R329 in the S6-RCK1 linker.
source: T11 of β4 is less than 5 Å away from D173 in the S2-S3 loop of the α subunit; the E12 sidechain of β4 is about 5.5 Å away from R329 in the S6-RCK1 linker and is also in the vicinity of W176 on S3 and H409 on the αC helix.
evidence: This is a distance measurement from the structural data.

claim: The E12 sidechain of β4 is in the vicinity of W176 on S3 and H409 on the αC helix.
source: T11 of β4 is less than 5 Å away from D173 in the S2-S3 loop of the α subunit; the E12 sidechain of β4 is about 5.5 Å away from R329 in the S6-RCK1 linker and is also in the vicinity of W176 on S3 and H409 on the αC helix.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The Slo1-β4 complex structure shows essentially no direct association between the β4 EC domain and the α subunit.
source: The Slo1-β4 complex structure shows essentially no direct association between the β4 EC domain and the α subunit.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data.

claim: The functional effects observed from mutations in the EC domain could be due to indirect effects.
source: The functional effects they observed from the mutations could be due to indirect effects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of direct contacts observed in the structure.

claim: β1 and β4 subunits slow the kinetics of Slo1 activation and deactivation in response to voltage steps.
source: β1 and β4 subunits slow the kinetics of Slo1 activation and deactivation in response to voltage steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4A.

claim: Mutants were made by replacing one or more of 10 regions of β4 mainly with the equivalent sequence from β1.
source: Mutants were made by replacing one or more of these 10 regions of β4 mainly with the equivalent sequence from β1 (Figure 4B and Table 2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the mutagenesis strategy.

claim: The β1 sequence was used instead of alanine or other substitutions, reasoning this would more likely achieve expression and assembly of a functional complex.
source: The β1 sequence – instead of alanine or other substitutions – was used, reasoning this would more likely achieve expression and assembly of a functional complex.
evidence: This is a methodological rationale.

claim: Mutants with faster activation rates were distributed throughout the β4 structure.
source: Mutants with faster activation rates were distributed throughout the β4 structure, while those with significantly slower activation rates were distributed with some bias towards the inner leaflet region of TM1, the N-loop, and the N-tail (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Mutants with significantly slower activation rates were distributed with some bias towards the inner leaflet region of TM1, the N-loop, and the N-tail.
source: Mutants with faster activation rates were distributed throughout the β4 structure, while those with significantly slower activation rates were distributed with some bias towards the inner leaflet region of TM1, the N-loop, and the N-tail (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: The N-tail plays a definitive role in determining activation kinetics.
source: Although not observed in the cryo-EM structure, the N-tail plays a definitive role in determining activation kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data from mutants.

claim: Mutants containing the N-tail of β4 activate more slowly than those with the N-tail of β1.
source: Specifically, mutants containing the N-tail of β4 activate more slowly than those with the N-tail of β1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The importance of the β subunit N-terminus to gating has already been proposed.
source: The importance of the β subunit N-terminus to gating has already been proposed (Castillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Removal of the N-tail results in a modest increase in the rate of activation.
source: We also observe that removal of the N-tail results in a modest increase in the rate of activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the functional data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The close proximity of the N-terminal region of the β4 subunit to the S6-RCK1 linker somehow underlies the effects on activation.
source: It would seem likely that the close proximity of this N-terminal region, including the N-tail of the β4 subunit, to an important gating region of the α subunit, the S6-RCK1 linker, somehow underlies the effects on activation that we observe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity and functional data.

claim: Ca2+ binding to two unique Ca2+ binding sites per α subunit produces protein conformational changes that splay the S6 (inner) helices, causing a wide pathway for ion diffusion to open between the cytoplasm and the transmembrane pore.
source: Ca2+ binding to two unique Ca2+ binding sites per α subunit produces protein conformational changes that splay the S6 (inner) helices, causing a wide pathway for ion diffusion to open between the cytoplasm and the transmembrane pore (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Ca2+ binding sites are located within the cytoplasmic 'gating ring', which is centered on the four-fold channel axis just beneath the transmembrane pore.
source: The Ca2+ binding sites are located within the cytoplasmic 'gating ring', which is centered on the four-fold channel axis just beneath the transmembrane pore (Figures 1B and 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 1B and 5B.

claim: When Ca2+ binds, a domain of the gating ring closest to the membrane, called the RCK1 N-lobe, expands away from the channel's central axis.
source: When Ca2+ binds, a domain of the gating ring closest to the membrane, called the RCK1 N-lobe, expands away from the channel's central axis; expansion of all four RCK1 N-lobes, one from each subunit, produces a radial expansion, as shown (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expansion of all four RCK1 N-lobes produces a radial expansion.
source: When Ca2+ binds, a domain of the gating ring closest to the membrane, called the RCK1 N-lobe, expands away from the channel's central axis; expansion of all four RCK1 N-lobes, one from each subunit, produces a radial expansion, as shown (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The RCK1 N-lobes are connected directly to the S6 helices via the S6-RCK1 linkers, and their expansion produces pore opening.
source: Since the RCK1 N-lobes are connected directly to the S6 helices via the S6-RCK1 linkers, their expansion produces pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural connectivity observed in the structure.

claim: Structural details of the Ca2+ binding site reorganization upon Ca2+ binding, RCK1 N-lobe expansion and pore opening observed in human Slo1 are essentially the same as those observed previously in acSlo1.
source: Structural details of the Ca2+ binding site reorganization upon Ca2+ binding, RCK1 N-lobe expansion and pore opening observed in human Slo1 are essentially the same as those observed previously in acSlo1 (Hite et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to prior structures and citations.

claim: The intricacies of Ca2+-mediated pore opening are conserved among Slo1 channels from invertebrates to mammals.
source: Thus, the intricacies of Ca2+-mediated pore opening are conserved among Slo1 channels from invertebrates to mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity between human and aplysia Slo1.

claim: The Ca2+-bound structures of the human Slo1 α subunit determined in the absence and presence of the β4 subunit are essentially identical to each other (RMSD 2.0 Å).
source: The Ca2+-bound structures of the human Slo1 α subunit determined in the absence and presence of the β4 subunit are essentially identical to each other (RMSD 2.0 Å) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two Ca2+-free structures of the α subunit (± β4 subunit) are also the same within the accuracy of measurements (RMSD 1.1 Å).
source: Likewise, the two Ca2+-free structures of the α subunit (± β4 subunit) are also the same within the accuracy of our measurements (RMSD 1.1 Å) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The β4 subunits encage the α subunit channel without interfering with its Ca2+-mediated gating conformational changes.
source: Contrasting the large Ca2+-mediated conformational changes that occur within the α subunit pore (Figure 5A) and gating ring (Figure 5B) with the absence of conformational change in the β4 subunit (Figure 5C) gives the impression that the β4 subunits encage the α subunit channel without interfering with its Ca2+-mediated gating conformational changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing no conformational change in β4.

claim: Within the outer leaflet of the membrane even lipid molecules that mediate interactions between the α and β subunits remain unperturbed.
source: Within the outer leaflet of the membrane even lipid molecules that mediate interactions between the α and β subunits remain unperturbed (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 5D and E.

claim: Within the inner leaflet of the membrane, where large gating conformational changes in the α subunit occur, interfaces between α and β subunits undergo change.
source: Within the inner leaflet of the membrane, where large gating conformational changes in the α subunit occur (Figure 5A and F–H), interfaces between α and β subunits – especially surrounding the more centrally located TM1 of the β subunit – undergo change.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 5A and F-H.

claim: In functional studies, β subunits alter the apparent Ca2+ sensitivity of gating.
source: In functional studies, β subunits alter the apparent Ca2+ sensitivity of gating.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The sensitivity changes are not thought to reflect changes in intrinsic Ca2+ affinity for the binding sites, but instead are proposed to reflect indirect effects that β subunits have on α subunit conformational changes that are coupled to Ca2+ binding.
source: But the sensitivity changes are not thought to reflect changes in intrinsic Ca2+ affinity for the binding sites, but instead are proposed to reflect indirect effects that β subunits have on α subunit conformational changes that are coupled to Ca2+ binding (Cox and Aldrich, 2000; Nimigean and Magleby, 2000; Bao and Cox, 2005; Savalli et al., 2007; Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The structures support the proposal that β subunits do not alter intrinsic Ca2+ affinity because the Ca2+ binding sites are unaltered by the presence of β subunits.
source: The structures support this proposal because the Ca2+ binding sites are unaltered by the presence of β subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: The 'weighting function' of conformational states would be altered by the presence of β subunits.
source: We expect that the 'weighting function' would be altered by the presence of β subunits.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The structural data support the idea that β subunits stabilize or destabilize conformational states of the α subunits rather than creating new states.
source: The structural data support the idea that β subunits stabilize or destabilize conformational states of the α subunits rather than creating new states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of identical conformations with and without β4.

claim: The RCK1 N-lobe and S6-RCK1 linker region of the α subunit is one likely region where β subunits exert their effects.
source: The RCK1 N-lobe and S6-RCK1 linker region of the α subunit is one likely region where β subunits exert their effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity and functional data.

claim: Direct stabilization of different conformations of voltage sensors by β subunits remains a distinct mechanistic possibility.
source: Direct stabilization of different conformations of voltage sensors by β subunits remains a distinct mechanistic possibility (Bao and Cox, 2005; Savalli et al., 2007; Contreras et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Certain protein toxins from scorpion venoms inhibit K+ channels by plugging their extracellular pore entryway.
source: Certain protein toxins from scorpion venoms inhibit K+ channels by plugging their extracellular pore entryway (Anderson et al., 1988; MacKinnon and Miller, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Understanding of these toxins' mechanism of action as pore blockers comes mainly from studies of charybdotoxin (CTX) and Iberiotoxin (IbTX) inhibition of Slo1 channels.
source: Our understanding of these toxins' mechanism of action as pore blockers comes mainly from studies of charybdotoxin (CTX) and Iberiotoxin (IbTX) inhibition of Slo1 channels (Candia et al., 1992; Giangiacomo et al., 1992; Miller, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The large conductance of Slo1 has enabled the measurement of toxin association and dissociation events in single channel recordings.
source: The large conductance of Slo1 has enabled the measurement of toxin association and dissociation events in single channel recordings (MacKinnon and Miller, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: About 30 years ago a Slo1 with altered toxin binding properties was discovered.
source: About 30 years ago a Slo1 with altered toxin binding properties was discovered (Reinhart et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The altered toxin binding properties were later attributed to the presence of β4 subunits.
source: The altered properties were later attributed to the presence of β4 subunits (Behrens et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2000; Meera et al., 2000; Weiger et al., 2000; Lippiat et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different β subunits confer unique pharmacological profiles to the Slo1 channel.
source: We now know that different β subunits confer unique pharmacological profiles to the Slo1 channel (Behrens et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2000; Lippiat et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies with mutant β subunits showed that toxins are most sensitive to the composition of the EC domain.
source: Studies with mutant β subunits showed that toxins are most sensitive to the composition of the EC domain (Meera et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The α-β4 structure provides a simple explanation for the general observation that β subunits slow the rates of association and dissociation of toxins with the channel: the EC domain crown limits access to the toxin binding site.
source: The α-β4 structure provides a simple explanation for the general observation that β subunits slow the rates of association and dissociation of toxins with the channel: the EC domain crown limits access to the toxin binding site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing the crown structure.

claim: There is adequate space for toxin binding within the cage beneath the crown.
source: Using the crystal structure of CTX bound to the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera channel to model CTX binding to Slo1, we conclude that there is adequate space for toxin binding within the cage beneath the crown, but that CTX has restricted access across the central opening to reach its binding site (Figure 6A–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Banerjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling using a prior crystal structure.

claim: CTX has restricted access across the central opening to reach its binding site.
source: Using the crystal structure of CTX bound to the Kv1.2-Kv2.1 paddle chimera channel to model CTX binding to Slo1, we conclude that there is adequate space for toxin binding within the cage beneath the crown, but that CTX has restricted access across the central opening to reach its binding site (Figure 6A–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) (Banerjee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural modeling using a prior crystal structure.

claim: The toxin is elongated along one axis and likely has to orient with its long axis parallel to the 4-fold axis to pass through the opening on the top of the crown.
source: The toxin is elongated along one axis and likely has to orient with its long axis parallel to the 4-fold axis to pass through the opening on the top of the crown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural modeling and dimensions of the toxin and crown opening.

claim: Optimal orientation will still require amino acid sidechain adjustments on both the toxin and β subunits to permit passage.
source: Optimal orientation will still require amino acid sidechain adjustments on both the toxin and β subunits to permit passage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural constraints.

claim: Restricted access rationalizes a reduced association rate if the probability of successful encounter is reduced.
source: Restricted access rationalizes a reduced association rate (compared to a Slo1 channel without β subunits) if the probability of successful encounter is reduced (Schurr, 1970).
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic theory and citation to prior literature.

claim: A reduced dissociation rate would reflect a reduced probability of toxin exit.
source: Analogously, a reduced dissociation rate would reflect a reduced probability of toxin exit.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic theory.

claim: If the toxin releases from its binding site and tumbles within the cage beneath the crown, rebinding many times before finally exiting, the resultant effect would be purely kinetic.
source: If the toxin releases from its binding site and tumbles within the cage beneath the crown, rebinding many times before finally exiting, the resultant effect would be purely kinetic (the assumption here being that release and rebinding without dissociation from the cage would be too rapid to resolve as dissociation events in channel recordings).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: If toxin is stabilized on its binding site by the β subunit, then equilibrium effects (i.e. effects on affinity) would also be expected.
source: If, on the other hand, toxin is stabilized on its binding site by the β subunit, then equilibrium effects (i.e. effects on affinity) would also be expected.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Data suggest that both kinetic and equilibrium effects occur.
source: Data suggest that both kinetic (i.e. rate changes that could be modeled through a barrier height) and equilibrium effects (i.e. affinity changes that could be modeled through the depth of a toxin binding well) occur (Behrens et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2000; Meera et al., 2000; Lippiat et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In 1994 Garcia and colleagues demonstrated that K69 on β1 (corresponding to R77 on β4) can be cross-linked to CTX.
source: In 1994 Garcia and colleagues demonstrated that K69 on β1 (corresponding to R77 on β4) can be cross-linked to CTX (Knaus et al., 1994a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: R77 is located inside the cage formed by the EC domain crown, facing the backside of CTX.
source: R77 is located inside the cage formed by the EC domain crown, facing the backside of CTX (i.e. the side opposite the pore's selectivity filter) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Scorpion toxins generally are electropositive on their surface: CTX and IbTX contain a total of 8 and 7 positively charged residues, respectively.
source: Scorpion toxins generally are electropositive on their surface: CTX and IbTX contain a total of 8 and 7 positively charged residues, respectively (Figure 6E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Garcia et. al. speculated that certain negatively charged residues within the large extracellular loop of the β subunit attract CTX to its binding site on the α subunit.
source: Garcia et. al. speculated that certain negatively charged residues within the large extracellular loop of the β subunit attract CTX to its binding site on the α subunit (Hanner et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The inner surface of the cage formed by the EC domain crown is electronegative due to the presence of two rings of negatively charged residues – E64 and E67.
source: In line with this hypothesis, the inner surface of the cage formed by the EC domain crown is electronegative due to the presence of two rings of negatively charged residues – E64 and E67 (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the structural data shown in Figures 6F-H.

claim: These positions (E64 and E67) are almost strictly conserved as negatively charged residues (E or D) in β1 to β4.
source: These positions are almost strictly conserved as negatively charged residues (E or D) in β1 to β4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which would create electrostatic interactions between the toxin and the β subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Conservation of E64 and E67 would create electrostatic interactions between the toxin and the β subunit.
source: These positions are almost strictly conserved as negatively charged residues (E or D) in β1 to β4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), which would create electrostatic interactions between the toxin and the β subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data and sequence conservation.

claim: Mutations made on the back side of CTX have little effect on affinity for Slo1 without β subunits.
source: Mutations made on the back side of CTX have little effect on affinity for Slo1 without β subunits (Park and Miller, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The structural model predicts that some of the same CTX mutations are likely to have an effect in the presence of β subunits.
source: The structural model predicts that some of the same CTX mutations are likely to have an effect in the presence of β subunits (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural model shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The structure offers a mechanistic picture explaining certain functional properties, such as the influence of β subunits on toxin interactions with Slo1.
source: The structure offers a mechanistic picture explaining certain functional properties, such as the influence of β subunits on toxin interactions with Slo1.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contributions of the structural data.

claim: The structure implies that the N-terminus of the β subunit TM1 and the segment of β4 preceding TM1 influence channel gating through interactions with the gating ring RCK1 N-lobe and the S6-RCK1 linker.
source: The structure also implies that the N-terminus of the β subunit TM1 and the segment of β4 preceding TM1 influence channel gating through interactions with the gating ring RCK1 N-lobe and the S6-RCK1 linker.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural proximity and functional data.

claim: The structure serves as an essential starting point for future understanding of unexplained functional properties.
source: For the unexplained properties, the structure still serves as an essential starting point for future understanding.
evidence: This is a general statement about the value of the structural data.

claim: The Slo1 β subunits are one example of relatively small membrane proteins that regulate the function of ion channels.
source: The Slo1 β subunits are one example of relatively small (i.e. TM segments not much larger than a few lipid molecules) membrane proteins that regulate the function of ion channels.
evidence: This is a general statement placing the findings in a broader context.

claim: KCNQ (Kv7) voltage-dependent K+ channels co-assemble with single membrane-spanning KCNE subunits.
source: Slo1 also has γ subunits, the KCNQ (Kv7) voltage-dependent K+ channels co-assemble with single membrane-spanning KCNE subunits, Kv4 co-assembles with dipeptidyl aminopeptidase-like (DPPL) proteins and voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels are also associated with auxiliary subunits (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010; Calhoun and Isom, 2014; Zhang and Yan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kv4 co-assembles with dipeptidyl aminopeptidase-like (DPPL) proteins.
source: Slo1 also has γ subunits, the KCNQ (Kv7) voltage-dependent K+ channels co-assemble with single membrane-spanning KCNE subunits, Kv4 co-assembles with dipeptidyl aminopeptidase-like (DPPL) proteins and voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels are also associated with auxiliary subunits (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010; Calhoun and Isom, 2014; Zhang and Yan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels are also associated with auxiliary subunits.
source: Slo1 also has γ subunits, the KCNQ (Kv7) voltage-dependent K+ channels co-assemble with single membrane-spanning KCNE subunits, Kv4 co-assembles with dipeptidyl aminopeptidase-like (DPPL) proteins and voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels are also associated with auxiliary subunits (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010; Calhoun and Isom, 2014; Zhang and Yan, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small transmembrane proteins are generally multifunctional, affecting various aspects of the larger target protein including trafficking/surface expression, biophysical properties, pharmacological profiles, and assembly into functional complexes.
source: These small transmembrane proteins are generally multifunctional, affecting various aspects of the larger target protein including trafficking/surface expression, biophysical properties, pharmacological profiles, and assembly into functional complexes (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010; Zickermann et al., 2010; Calhoun and Isom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DPPL for Kv4 has been implicated in binding to components of the extracellular matrix through its extracellular domain.
source: DPPL for Kv4 has been implicated in binding to components of the extracellular matrix through its extracellular domain (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010), and the Nav β subunit extracellular domain plays a crucial role in cell adhesion and migration (Calhoun and Isom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Nav β subunit extracellular domain plays a crucial role in cell adhesion and migration.
source: DPPL for Kv4 has been implicated in binding to components of the extracellular matrix through its extracellular domain (Pongs and Schwarz, 2010), and the Nav β subunit extracellular domain plays a crucial role in cell adhesion and migration (Calhoun and Isom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Whether the structured crown of Slo1 β subunits interacts with extracellular matrix proteins to localize Slo1 channels to specific regions of a cell is still unknown.
source: Whether the structured crown of Slo1 β subunits (sequence similarity virtually guarantees a similar extracellular structure in β1-β3 as well) interacts with extracellular matrix proteins to localize Slo1 channels to specific regions of a cell, perhaps regions of contact with other cells, is still unknown, but seems like a good possibility.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible function of the crown structure.

claim: Sequence similarity virtually guarantees a similar extracellular structure in β1-β3 as well as β4.
source: Whether the structured crown of Slo1 β subunits (sequence similarity virtually guarantees a similar extracellular structure in β1-β3 as well) interacts with extracellular matrix proteins to localize Slo1 channels to specific regions of a cell, perhaps regions of contact with other cells, is still unknown, but seems like a good possibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence similarity.

claim: When β subunit TM helices encircle the α subunit, they must displace lipid molecules.
source: Another idea we have when looking at the α-β4 Slo1 structure is inspired by the location of the β subunit TM helices. When they encircle the α subunit, they must displace lipid molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement.

claim: The presence of β subunits necessitates the displacement of some lipids.
source: As shown in the structures, certain lipid molecules are bound at the α/β subunit interfaces, but the presence of β subunits necessitates the displacement of some lipids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The function of many ion channels is very sensitive to the membrane lipid composition.
source: We know that the function of many ion channels is very sensitive to the membrane lipid composition (Heginbotham et al., 1998; Valiyaveetil et al., 2002; Schmidt et al., 2006; Schmidt et al., 2009; Cheng et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is useful to view small transmembrane spanning proteins as membrane components that, like lipids, by altering the chemical and physical properties of the surrounding membrane, alter the function of the ion channel.
source: Thus, we consider it perhaps useful to view these small transmembrane spanning proteins as membrane components that, like lipids, by altering the chemical and physical properties of the surrounding membrane, alter the function of the ion channel.
